title: TypeScript versus JavaScript and C#
hook: TypeScript versus JavaScript and C# shows up in everyday TypeScript and in senior interviews — this page explains what it is, why it matters, and how it behaves in the compiler versus JavaScript or C#.

blocks.text: TypeScript versus JavaScript and C# is a core concept in TypeScript. At run time, types erase — the engine still executes JavaScript — but at compile time this concept shapes safe APIs and catches bugs before deploy. This page explains the idea in plain English first, then shows small, explained examples you can run in the browser console or Node.js.

entries.plainDefinition: The central idea behind "TypeScript versus JavaScript and C#" — how it appears in source code and what the compiler does with it.
entries.example: See the code walkthrough section for a minimal working example.

entries.plainDefinition: The official specification that JavaScript implements. TypeScript is a typed superset that compiles to ECMAScript.
entries.example: const, classes, and async/await are ECMAScript features.

blocks.text: Senior interviews and production code both probe whether you understand TypeScript versus JavaScript and C# beyond syntax memorization. Misunderstanding here leads to subtle bugs — wrong equality results, leaked memory, untyped JSON boundaries, or async ordering surprises. If you know JavaScript, the comparison sections below help you transfer mental models instead of starting from zero.

blocks.title: Interview trap
blocks.body: Interviewers often ask "TypeScript versus JavaScript and C#" as a follow-up to a coding exercise. They want mechanism and tradeoffs — not a one-line definition.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Treating TypeScript versus JavaScript and C# as pure syntax without run-time behavior. Skipping validation at JSON or API boundaries. Saying "it works on my machine" without noting browser versus Node differences.
